lead: A solid expands when heated because its atoms vibrate over slightly larger distances. The change in length is proportional to the original length and to the temperature rise. A rail, bridge or pipeline must be allowed to move by that much. If the ends are clamped, the blocked expansion appears as thermal stress. The same effect bends a bimetallic strip, which switches a thermostat. Only a few universities teach the bimetallic strip in detail. This chapter gives the three standard results and the numbers engineers use.
prereq: You need: 1.2 — stress, strain and Young's modulus, because thermal stress is a strain held back by the material.

blocks.text: A rod of original length L at temperature T expands by ΔL when its temperature rises by ΔT. The rule is ΔL = L α ΔT. α is the coefficient of linear expansion, the fractional length change per degree Celsius. Its unit is per °C; the number is the same per K because only a temperature difference enters. For a thin sheet, area grows by ΔA = A β ΔT with β ≈ 2α. For a solid block, volume grows by ΔV = V γ ΔT with γ ≈ 3α. These are small-change approximations for an isotropic solid, one whose properties are the same in every direction.

blocks.where: L is original length in m; ΔL is change in length in m; α is coefficient of linear expansion in per °C; ΔT is temperature change in °C or K.

blocks.text: If both ends of a rod are fixed, the free expansion LαΔT is blocked. The material is compressed by the same strain that heating would have produced: strain = αΔT. Hooke's law then gives thermal stress σ = Y α ΔT, where Y is Young's modulus in N/m². The force on the supports is F = σA, with A the cross-section area in m². Stress does not depend on length; force does. A rail, bridge deck or pipeline therefore needs an expansion gap of at least LαΔT, and a bridge girder rests on roller supports at one end.

items: Bimetallic strip: two metals with different α are bonded.
On heating, the larger-α side becomes longer and lies on the outside of the bend.
The curvature grows with ΔT and with the difference α₁ − α₂.
It is used in thermostats, fire alarms and old clocks.

figure.caption: Brass expands more than iron. The bonded pair curves on heating, with brass on the outside of the bend; the same strip is used in a thermostat.

spec.aria: Two bonded layers, brass on top and iron below; on heating the brass expands more and the strip curves with the brass on the outside.

examples.question: A steel rail is 20 m long and clamped at both ends at 25 °C. α = 12×10⁻⁶ per °C, Y = 2.0×10¹¹ Pa. The hottest day reaches 55 °C. (a) Find the gap an expansion joint must allow. (b) Find the thermal stress if the rail cannot move.
steps: Free expansion ΔL = LαΔT = 20 × 12×10⁻⁶ × 30 = 7.2×10⁻³ m = 7.2 mm.
examples.answer: The expansion joint must allow 7.2 mm; if blocked, the rail carries 72 MPa of thermal stress.
examples.check:
L = 20.0
alpha = 12e-6
Y = 2.0e11
dT = 55 - 25
gap_mm = L * alpha * dT * 1000
stress_MPa = Y * alpha * dT / 1e6
print(gap_mm)
print(stress_MPa)

traps: ΔT is the change, not the temperature. From 25 °C to 55 °C, ΔT = 30 °C, not 55 °C. The same number works in kelvin.
A coefficient quoted per °F is smaller than the per °C value; convert before putting it into LαΔT.
β ≈ 2α and γ ≈ 3α hold for an isotropic solid, not for a long rod where only length matters.
Thermal stress YαΔT is independent of length and area. Force σA depends on area, so a thicker rail carries more force at the same stress.
In a heated bimetallic strip, the larger-α metal is on the outside of the curve, not the inside.

quiz.q: Define the coefficient of linear expansion and give its SI unit.
quiz.a: α = (1/L)(ΔL/ΔT); unit per °C or per K.

quiz.q: Why does a bimetallic strip bend when heated?
quiz.a: The two bonded metals have different α. The larger-α side expands more, becomes longer, and lies outside the curve.

quiz.q: A 5.0 m aluminium rod (α = 23×10⁻⁶ /°C) warms from 20 °C to 50 °C. Find ΔL.
A clamped steel rod is replaced by a rod of the same material and cross-section but twice the length. ΔT is unchanged. Compare the thermal stress and the force on the supports.
quiz.a: Stress σ = YαΔT is unchanged because it does not contain L. Force F = σA is also unchanged because A is unchanged.

quiz.q: A brass rod has α = 19×10⁻⁶ /°C, Y = 1.0×10¹¹ Pa, A = 2.0×10⁻⁴ m², and ΔT = 40 °C. It is clamped at both ends. Find the stress and the force.
Why do bridge girders rest on roller supports at one end?
quiz.a: To allow the girder to expand and contract freely, so thermal stress does not build up.

beyond: Not for the exam. Railways use continuously welded rails with pretension and expansion joints; bridges use bearings and gaps. Cryogenic tanks and space structures match α of joined materials to avoid thermal stress. Bimetallic strips survive in cheap thermostats and overload trips. Search: thermal expansion coefficient, thermal stress, bimetallic thermostat, expansion joint design.
